title: Engineering Better Evals: Scalable LLM Evaluation Pipelines That Work — Dat Ngo, Aman Khan, Arize
talk_summary: Arize engineers describe evals as a layered toolbox (code/heuristic checks, encoder-only classifiers, LLM-as-judge, human labels) and stress tuning the judge itself against a golden set. They also cover agent-specific evals: conditional evals on control flow, trajectory evals against reference paths, and aggregate path analysis across traces to find failure modes.

takeaways.technique: Cheap-first eval ladder (code > encoder > LLM judge)
takeaways.what_they_do: Use deterministic code checks (regex, JSON parse, keyword presence) and small encoder-only classifiers before spending an LLM call on judging; reserve LLM-as-judge for what only it can assess.
takeaways.evidence_quote: things like encoder only BERT type architectures are super helpful. They're about 10 times cheaper um about one or two orders of magnitudes faster
takeaways.numbers: encoder-only evals ~10x cheaper, 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than LLM judges

takeaways.technique: Calibrate the LLM judge against a golden set
takeaways.what_they_do: Hand-label a small golden set of known-good/known-bad cases, run the LLM judge on it, and tune the judge prompt until it approximates human labels; keep collecting judge failures and re-tuning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can run your LM as a judge on a golden data set ... can the LLM approximate the thing that I trust

takeaways.technique: Conditional evals on control flow first
takeaways.what_they_do: If an agent has branching/control flow, evaluate whether the correct path was taken before evaluating downstream outputs, since downstream evals are wasted if routing was wrong.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you didn't get the control flow right, why eval anything down the line? Because it's probably wrong

takeaways.what_they_do: Define expected tool/component sequences for a task, then grade actual trajectories either by exact path match or by passing expected-vs-actual paths to an LLM; also aggregate path distributions across many runs to find which path correlates with failures.
takeaways.evidence_quote: here's the trajectory that I hit ... here's the possible paths ... Did I do well in these specific areas

takeaways.technique: Guardrails are for known-knowns; fix the prompt, not the guardrail
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat inline guardrails like unit tests for known failure classes; when something slips through, fix the root-cause prompt/orchestration rather than loosening or patching the guardrail.
takeaways.evidence_quote: people mistake guardrails as like the thing that needs to be adjusted ... you need to adjust system one. That's the root cause

takeaways.what_they_do: Feed input/output pairs plus eval pass/fail labels and the current prompt to an LLM, asking it to produce a revised prompt that fixes the failing cases.
takeaways.evidence_quote: here's the input output pairs here's the eval on those things ... can you give me a new prompt that fixes this data set
